Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
On 1 Nov 1996, ro...@duke.usask.ca (Nicole Roy) wrote:
>Rules Questions
>---------------
>Hidden Pathways: Define 'directed at your prey'. Do damaging votes count?
>(I'm assuming that they do not; you are not supposed to name the target
>of a vote until it is unblocked, after which point this card would be
>useless. At the same time, I find nothing which prevents you from doing
>so in advance...)

An action is "directed at your prey" if it is a directed action and the
target is your Prey (including actions directed at a card or cards controlled
by your Prey).

>Mind of a Child: Is the action to burn this card (D) or Undirected?

It is undirected.

Although by the definition of directed, the action should be directed when
attempted by a vampire controlled by a Methuselah other than the controller
of the victim of Mind of a Child (who is thus the controller of Mind of a
Child itself), the Rules Team has clearly indicated that this definition
is only a guideline. The only thing that determines the directedness of
an action is the presence or absence of the (D) symbol on the card text
(or in errata, in the cases where card text is in error in an obvious way).

(Precedent set by The Treatment.)

>My Enemy's Enemy: Just double checking on this one. If I am understanding
>correctly, you can end up bleeding yourself in a three-person game.
>Doesn't this break some sort of fundamental rule? And if you _do_ end up
>bleeding yourself, can you have one of your vampires attempt to block it?

No, in a three-player game, if your Predator is bleeding you and you play
My Enemy's Enemy, then she is now bleeding your Predator's Predator, i.e.,
her Predator, i.e., your Prey.

--

If your Prey plays MEE, the you are the one who is taking the action,

Just to rephrase what Scott is saying: the card text on MEE prohibits
playing the card unless you are being bled by your predator's minion, so
in your example your prey can't play MEE in response to a misdirected bleed
from your predator (which would otherwise result in a self-bleed).

L. Scott Johnson (vte...@wizards.com) wrote:

: If your Prey plays MEE, the you are the one who is taking the action,

: so your Predator won't be bleeding anyone at all.

: MEE cannot, under any contrivance, possibly indicate that someone

I _think_ I'm the one that wrote the original question, long long ago when
Sabbat first came out. If so, I mis-read the card, and mis-asked the
question. So, while my original question has no relevance, is there not
still a case where the vampire can end up bleeding its owner--namely, a
2-player game?

My Enemy's Enemy Reaction Auspex
Normal: +1 intercept
Superior: Only usable when a minion controlled by your predator attempts
to bleed you. Tap this reacting vampire. The minion is now bleeding
your predator's predator.
Artist: Dave Seeley Rarity: Rare

A: "Ozmo bleeds."
B: "Block with Anneke"
A: Proceeds to play more stealth than B has intercept.
B: Plays 'My Enemy's Enemy'

Ozmo should now be bleeding the predator of A's predator... namely, the
predator of B... namely A.

Wnat am I missing about this situation that makes outside the realm of
possible contrivance?

Seems to me that MEE is the _only_ bleed-bounce card which is useful in a
two-player game, as the rest of them all state that the bleed cannot be
bounced back to the acting Meth. As there is no such restriction printed
on this card, I reiterate my question:
-- Is there anything fundamental about the bleed action which prevents it
it from being redirected back at the acting Methuselah?
-- If so, why? (since card text is quite plain here...)
-- If not, is there anything fundamental about the redirection process
which either allows or the acting Methuselah to attempt to block
his own minion with another or prevents him from doing so?
